title: How I Built the Contact Form on jasontang.dev
subtitle: how i mastered playing hard to get
source:
One of the smaller features on my portfolio that was surprisingly fun to build was the contact form.

I was inspired by [vert.nyc](https://www.vert.nyc/), where you have to beat a game of Snake to get their email. So I decided to play hard to get too, even though my email is pretty easy to find elsewhere.

On my site, you have to beat Breakout first. Once you win, a Mail window opens and you can send me a message without leaving the page.

**TL;DR:** the frontend sends the message to a Cloudflare Worker, the Worker checks it, and Cloudflare delivers it to my Gmail. No SMTP server, and no email password stored anywhere in the site.

![Sequence diagram: the visitor types a message, Mail.vue posts it to /api/contact, the Worker validates it and hands it to Email Routing, which delivers it to Gmail](/api/blog/images/a58252be59c98f98d440ed11fc8d5aaf59076245eba9f16e0b4b54173605936e.png "The whole trip, from Send to my inbox")

# Sending from the frontend

When someone clicks **Send**, the Mail window makes a `POST` request to `/api/contact` with their name, email and message, plus two extra fields I'll get to in the spam section.

The Worker checks everything before it sends anything. The name, email and message all have to be there, the email has to look like an email, and each one has a length limit (5,000 characters for the message).

It also replaces line breaks and other control characters in the name and email with spaces. Those two values end up in the email's headers, and a sneaky line break there could add headers of its own. That's called header injection.

If anything goes wrong, the Worker returns an error, the Mail window shows it, and the message stays in the box so the visitor can try again instead of typing it all out a second time.

# Lightweight spam protection

I didn't want a CAPTCHA on a small portfolio form, so there are three cheap checks instead.

The first is a hidden `website` field. Real visitors never see it, but basic bots tend to fill in every input they find. If it has anything in it, the Worker says the message was sent and quietly drops it. A bot that thinks it succeeded has no reason to try again.

The second is `elapsed`, which tracks how long the Mail window was open before Send was clicked. Bots can fill forms instantly and people usually take a few seconds, so anything under three seconds is turned away. At first those submissions got the same fake success as the honeypot, but that meant a fast human could lose their message without knowing. Now they get a "wait a few seconds and try again" error instead.

The third is an `Origin` check. The Worker only accepts browser requests coming from `jasontang.dev`, so another website can't quietly post to the form from a visitor's browser.

None of these are airtight. A script can fake the timing or leave out the `Origin` header, and the server never checks that you actually beat Breakout. The game is part of the fun, not a security boundary.

# Sending through Cloudflare

The actual send is pretty small:

```js
const raw = buildEmail(result.data, {
  from,
  to,
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
});

await env.SEND_EMAIL.send(
  new EmailMessage(from, to, raw)
);
```

`SEND_EMAIL` is a Cloudflare binding. It's set up in `wrangler.jsonc` and handed to the Worker at runtime:

```json
{
  "send_email": [
    {
      "name": "SEND_EMAIL",
      "destination_address": "jasontcanada@gmail.com"
    }
  ]
}
```

That means I don't store any email credentials myself, and the Worker can only ever send to that one verified address. Even if someone found a bug in my code, they couldn't use it to email anyone else.

Some of the setup lives outside the repo. Email Routing has to be turned on for `jasontang.dev`, its DNS records have to exist, and my Gmail address has to be verified as a destination in Cloudflare. Once that's done, the Worker hands the email off and Cloudflare handles delivery.

I also chose not to save submissions in a database or KV. For the traffic a portfolio contact form gets, keeping a second copy of every message felt unnecessary. Gmail is the storage.

![Diagram: the visitor's message goes to the Cloudflare Worker, then through Email Routing to Gmail, with a dotted line to a database that isn't there](/api/blog/images/9bb002127d9596a84bf4b3d1b753e85e01f9bba6d3e0a8f5a538f5ee1e8d46a5.png "Straight through to Gmail, no database on the side")

# HOW did you get my email????

`buildEmail` writes the raw email by hand: the headers first, then the message as a Base64 body. The most interesting choice in there is who the email is *from*.

The obvious idea is to make it come from the visitor, so it looks like they emailed me directly. That doesn't work. Gmail checks whether an email claiming to be from a domain was actually sent by servers authorized by that domain. That's what SPF, DKIM and DMARC are for.

A message claiming to be from `someone@gmail.com` that actually came out of Cloudflare can fail those checks, so it may get flagged as spoofed, land in spam, or bounce.

So the email comes from `contact@jasontang.dev`, an address on my own domain that Cloudflare is set up to send for, and the visitor's address goes in the `Reply-To` header.

When I hit Reply in Gmail, it goes straight to them. Their name is also in the subject line, so my inbox still shows who wrote in, and names with accents are encoded so they survive the trip through the email headers.

# Takeaways

The email send itself is only a few lines. Most of the work is everything around it: validating requests, preventing header injection, basic spam protection, picking the right From address, setting up DNS and Email Routing, and making sure failures are handled properly.

From the visitor's side, it's *type a message, click Send.*

Behind the scenes:

```text
Vue → HTTP → Cloudflare Worker → MIME → Email Routing → DNS → Gmail
```

It's a small feature, but it ended up touching the frontend, backend, infrastructure, DNS and email delivery all at once.
